Paths and display logic

Source: vignettes/paths-and-display-logic.Rmd
paths-and-display-logic.Rmd

What this answers. How the paths through a survey are reconstructed, and what the structural profile’s weights mean.

What you need. A .qsf.

What it cannot establish. The structural profile is not a respondent distribution; branch conditions are not checked against each other, so its extremes may be unreachable.

This article covers how surveyBurden reconstructs the paths through a survey and turns them into a burden spread, and the difference between the structural profile and respondent burden. For per-question scoring see vignette("gfs-scoring"); for the printed output see vignette("reading-the-report").

library(surveyBurden)
#> 
#>                   .-- Q2 -- Q3 --.
#>   survey -- Q1 --+               +-- Burden 0.3.0
#>                   '-- Q4 --------'
#> 
#> An R package for assessing the response-burden of web surveys
#> Docs: https://pmpk20.github.io/surveyBurden/
#> 
#> Please cite: King P (2026). surveyBurden: An R package for assessing
#> the response-burden of web surveys. R package version 0.3.0,
#> https://github.com/pmpk20/surveyBurden.
#> Use citation("surveyBurden") for BibTeX.
demo <- system.file("extdata", "demo_travel_survey.qsf", package = "surveyBurden")
qsf <- read_qsf(demo)
report <- burden_report(demo, quiet = TRUE)

Survey flow

Contemporary web surveys are not a fixed sequence. resolve_flow() walks the SurveyFlow, forking at every Branch into a condition-true and a condition-false continuation, and at every EndSurvey into a screen-out. Branch conditions mostly depend on embedded data or prior answers that are unknown before fieldwork, so both outcomes are kept. The exception is a branch that compares one embedded field with a value (=, !=, >, >=, <, <=): the field holds one value along a path, so every branch on it agrees with that value, and a fixed value set earlier in the flow (including one a randomiser picks) decides the branch. A run of equality tests on one field (“group is 1”, “group is 2”, …) becomes one path per value plus a “none matches” path, because the field could hold any value. When you know the values a field can hold, declare them:

burden_report(qsf, field_domains = list(group = c("1", "2")))

The “none matches” path is then dropped unless a declared value matches no branch. The result is every block sequence a respondent could encounter.

resolve_flow(qsf)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   path_id block_ids  terminates_early decisions
#>     <int> <list>     <lgl>            <list>   
#> 1       1 <chr [2]>  TRUE             <lgl [1]>
#> 2       2 <chr [3]>  TRUE             <lgl [2]>
#> 3       3 <chr [12]> FALSE            <lgl [3]>
#> 4       4 <chr [11]> FALSE            <lgl [3]>
nrow(report$paths)
#> [1] 4
sum(report$paths$status == "complete")
#> [1] 2
sum(report$paths$status == "screen_out")
#> [1] 2

A block randomiser that shows m of its M elements (“present 1 of 3 blocks”) is enumerated as one path per combination of elements, each in survey order; order does not change burden. With even presentation each combination is equally likely, which matches the equal weight each path gets. When the number shown cannot be read, every element is treated as shown, with a warning. A randomiser holding only embedded-data assignments shows nothing; it adds paths only when a later branch tests a field it sets (one path per value it can assign). The path space is enumerated up to max_paths (10000); a flow that would produce more raises an error rather than a partial answer.

Display logic

Within a path, resolve_paths() partitions the questions into three sets: always shown, may be shown (gated by a condition that cannot be evaluated before fieldwork), and never shown on this path (the gate’s trigger question is not on the path).

rp <- resolve_paths(qsf)
data.frame(
  path_id    = rp$path_id,
  screen_out = rp$terminates_early,
  n_always   = lengths(rp$q_always),
  n_maybe    = lengths(rp$q_maybe),
  n_gates    = rp$n_gates
)
#>   path_id screen_out n_always n_maybe n_gates
#> 1       1       TRUE        2       0       0
#> 2       2       TRUE        3       0       0
#> 3       3      FALSE       20       6       4
#> 4       4      FALSE       20       3       3

Qualtrics display logic is stored as If / ElseIf / AndIf groups. The package folds each group left to right: ElseIf clauses combined with OR, AndIf clauses with AND, a missing type falling back to AND. Flattening everything to AND would under-count the cases where a question appears if any one of several conditions holds.

Path enumeration

path_burden_profile() goes inside the “may be shown” set and enumerates the display-logic states the package can model.

  • Conditional questions are grouped into coupling components: two questions couple if they share a gate, directly or through a chain of shared gates.
  • A component with at most max_condition_states (default 10000) joint gate-states is enumerated in full – every joint state of its gates that the model represents, respecting single-choice mutual exclusion and AND-across-gates conditions. A stored (embedded data) field compared with EqualTo, NotEqualTo or an inequality is enumerated over its distinguishable values, so conditions on different values of one field are mutually exclusive. “In full” means exhaustive within the model: a field compared with any other operator is still treated as a free true/false condition, and branch conditions are not checked against display logic.
  • A larger component (dozens of questions keyed off one popular trigger such as employment status) falls back to a primary-gate approximation: each question is scored against its first gate, the rest held permissive.
  • Separate components are convolved as independent.
  • Loop & Merge blocks are unrolled to the explicit ?v=N cap, with the iteration count treated as uniform over 1 to N in the structural profile, unless loop_weights gives other weights (for example loop_weights = list(BL_x = c(1, 1, 1, 9))).
  • Display logic inside a loop is evaluated. A trigger in the same loop block is answered afresh in each iteration; a trigger outside the block (an earlier question or a stored field) has one answer for every iteration, shared with any non-loop question that uses it; a “Loop 1 … Current Loop” condition holds in the first iteration only.
  • A trigger question that is not shown is unanswered, so nothing appears because of an answer to a question that was never displayed. A shown trigger whose response is forced has no unanswered state (respect_force_response = TRUE, the default).
pbp <- path_burden_profile(qsf)
pbp[, c("path_id", "terminates_early", "burden_min",
        "burden_median", "burden_max")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   path_id terminates_early burden_min burden_median burden_max
#>     <int> <lgl>                 <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1       1 TRUE                     12            12         12
#> 2       2 TRUE                     14            14         14
#> 3       3 FALSE                   103           121        143
#> 4       4 FALSE                   103           119        139
nrow(pbp$profile[[3]])   # distinct modelled burden values on complete path 3
#> [1] 41

Each row of a profile table is one modelled burden value with a structural weight: each joint gate state and each loop iteration count gets equal weight, a value produced by several states carries their combined weight, and the weights on a path sum to 1. That weight is a model weight, not a respondent probability.

Burden by block for each traversal

path_burden_traversals() returns the traversals behind the profile: one row per traversal and block, with points, items, response items and pages, so a cumulative-by-block curve and the totals come from the same weighted traversals. Small surveys are enumerated exactly; larger ones are sampled with a fixed seed (traversal_stability() reports the spread across seeds). field_rules can derive stored fields that survey code computes, which the survey file does not record.

tr <- path_burden_traversals(qsf, method = "exact")
head(tr[, c("traversal_id", "path_id", "weight", "block_id", "points")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   traversal_id path_id  weight block_id points
#>          <int>   <int>   <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1            1       3 0.00139 BL1          11
#> 2            1       3 0.00139 BL2           1
#> 3            1       3 0.00139 BL3           2
#> 4            1       3 0.00139 BL4          15
#> 5            1       3 0.00139 BL5           3
#> 6            1       3 0.00139 BL6           4

Structural versus respondent burden

This distinction is central and is easy to state wrongly.

The default result is a structural burden profile. It covers the combinations of optional questions the package can model, weighted by the model: each complete path carries equal total weight, and within a path each modelled combination does. It carries no respondent probabilities. When the report says the median is 120 points, it means the median of that model-weighted distribution. It does not mean half of respondents face at least that much burden. Nobody has told the package how common each path or combination is.

For a distribution across respondents, supply response data: burden_report(qsf, responses = ...) adds $respondents, quantiles and the mean of respondent burden over complete responses. Each respondent counts once, so paths taken by more respondents carry more weight. See vignette("respondent-burden") for the measure and the data it needs.
